On **voting Sunday**, polling stations are usually only open in the **morning**. In some municipalities you can also go on the Saturday or on another day beforehand. When the polling station closes, the **counting** of the votes begins. The results then become known in the afternoon or evening.

If you want to vote, you take your **voting card** with you. The members of the **electoral office** check it. This shows that you are entitled to vote. Then you fill in your ballot paper behind a **screen** or in a booth. Finally you put it in the sealed **ballot box**.

At the polling station everyone should be able to decide in peace. That is why nobody may **campaign** there for yes or no. The screen makes sure that nobody is watching. This keeps the **secrecy of the ballot**. Each voter has only **one vote** per proposal.

Today most people in Switzerland vote **by post**. But the polling station remains important for everyone who likes to vote in person. Anyone who has already voted by post may not vote again at the polling station. Otherwise the result would be distorted.

gewusst: The expression “going to the ballot box” is often used even when someone votes by post.
The members of the electoral office are usually people from the municipality itself who take on this task.

teile.einleitung: Clean streets and squares make a municipality nicer and safer. The municipality's staff take care of this with brooms and machines. But all residents can help too.
wichtigste: The municipality's public works service or depot keeps the streets clean.
The road sweeper cleans streets and pavements with rotating brushes.
In autumn a particularly large amount of leaves is cleared away.
At the Robidog there are little bags for dog poo.
Anyone who puts rubbish in the bin saves the municipality work and money.
On Clean-up Day many people collect rubbish voluntarily.

abschnitte.text: In a municipality the **public works service** or **depot** is usually responsible for cleanliness. The staff sweep streets, squares and pavements. They also empty the public **litter bins**, for example at bus stops. Otherwise full bins would overflow.

For large areas there is the **road sweeper**, also called a **sweeping machine**. It has **rotating brushes** that sweep up dust, leaves and rubbish. A vacuum sucks the dirt into a container. The machine often sprays a little water as it goes, so that less dust is stirred up.

In **autumn** lots of leaves fall from the trees. Wet **leaves** can be slippery and are therefore cleared away. After a **village festival** there is often a lot of rubbish lying around. Then the municipality or helpers usually clean up **the very next day**.

The green **Robidog** is known all over Switzerland. Little **bags** for dog poo hang on it. Dog owners use them to pick up their dog's poo and put the bag in the box. That way paths and meadows stay clean.

If nobody throws rubbish on the ground, the municipality stays clean. Dropping rubbish outdoors is called **littering**. In many places there is a **fine** for it. On **Clean-up Day** many people voluntarily collect rubbish in nature and in the municipality, and school classes take part too.

gewusst: The Robidog was invented in Switzerland.
In winter the public works service also clears snow and spreads salt or grit so that nobody slips.

teile.einleitung: Every Swiss canton has its own government. In most cantons it is called the Regierungsrat. It runs the affairs of the canton, much as the Federal Council does for the Confederation.
wichtigste: The Regierungsrat is the government of a canton.
It is elected by the people.
A cantonal government almost always has 5 or 7 members.
In Zurich and Bern, the cantonal government has 7 members each.
Each member heads a directorate, similar to a department.
A term of office usually lasts 4 years.

abschnitte.text: The **Regierungsrat** is the government, that is the executive branch, of a canton. It puts into practice the laws passed by the cantonal parliament and runs the cantonal administration. Unlike the Federal Council, which is elected by parliament, the cantonal government is **elected by the people** in all cantons. It works as a **collegial body**: the members decide together and stand by their decisions together in public.

A cantonal government almost always consists of **5 or 7 members**. In large cantons such as **Zurich** and **Bern** there are **7**. Each member heads a **directorate**, called a department in some cantons. There is, for example, a directorate for education, one for health and one for finance. It is chaired by a president, who usually changes **every year**.

The government is not called Regierungsrat everywhere. In **Geneva** and other French-speaking cantons it is called the **Conseil d'État**, meaning council of state. In Ticino it is called the Consiglio di Stato. In **Appenzell Innerrhoden** the government is called the **Standeskommission**. Its chairman there has the title Landammann. In other cantons, too, people speak of the Landammann or the president of the government.

A term of office in the cantonal government usually lasts **4 years**, and 5 years in some cantons. In most cantons the election uses the **majority system**. Those who are elected can stand for election again afterwards. In many cantons several parties are represented in the government, similar to the Federal Council.

gewusst: In the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, the government is elected in the open air at the Landsgemeinde, the cantonal assembly.
The canton of Ticino is one of the few cantons that elect their government by proportional representation.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who launches a popular initiative can withdraw it again under certain conditions. Then no popular vote takes place. Committees often do this when parliament meets them halfway with a counter-proposal.
wichtigste: Withdrawal is possible until the Federal Council sets the date of the vote.
An absolute majority of the initiative committee decides on the withdrawal.
Every signature list must contain a withdrawal clause.
An initiative is often withdrawn because of a counter-proposal.
A conditional withdrawal only applies if the indirect counter-proposal comes into force.
Conditional withdrawal has existed at federal level since 2010.

abschnitte.text: Every signature list for a popular initiative contains a **withdrawal clause**. It is compulsory. That way everyone who signs knows that the **initiative committee** may withdraw the initiative later. A withdrawal requires an **absolute majority** of the committee members who are still entitled to vote, in other words more than half.

abschnitte.titel: Until when can it be withdrawn?
abschnitte.text: A withdrawal is possible until the **Federal Council has set the date of the vote**. After that, the initiative will definitely go to the people. A withdrawal is **final**. Anyone who wants to bring the same proposal again later has to launch a new initiative and collect 100,000 signatures once more.

Parliament can put forward a **counter-proposal** to an initiative. If this at least partly fulfils the aim, many committees withdraw their initiative. That way they avoid the risk of losing everything in a vote. They secure a **partial success**.

Since 2010 there has been **conditional withdrawal** at federal level. It only applies if the **indirect counter-proposal**, that is a law, really comes into force. If a referendum is called against this law and the law is rejected, the initiative still goes to a vote after all. One example is the **organ donation initiative**: the people accepted the opt-out solution on 15 May 2022, and the withdrawal became final.

gewusst: Quite a lot of popular initiatives never come to a vote, because they are withdrawn.
Conditional withdrawal was introduced through an amendment to the Federal Act on Political Rights.

teile.einleitung: An electoral threshold is a hurdle in proportional elections. Parties that receive less than a certain share of the votes get no seats in parliament. Many countries have such hurdles; Switzerland does not in the National Council elections.
wichtigste: A threshold is meant to prevent a **fragmented parliament**.
In Germany the **five per cent hurdle** applies in elections to the Bundestag.
With three directly won seats, a party still gets into the Bundestag (as of 2025).
Parties of national minorities such as the **SSW** are exempt from the hurdle.
Since 2014 Israel has had a hurdle of 3.25 per cent.
In Switzerland a **natural hurdle** arises in small cantons.

abschnitte.text: In a **proportional election**, parties receive as many seats as their share of the votes. Without a hurdle, a great many small parties could enter parliament. Then it is difficult to form stable majorities and a government that can act. An **electoral threshold** is meant to prevent this. Critics, on the other hand, say that this means many votes have no effect.

In elections to the Bundestag, a party needs at least **5 per cent** of the second votes. But if it wins at least three constituencies directly, it is still counted according to its share of the votes. In 2024 the Federal Constitutional Court let this **basic mandate clause** continue to apply until new rules are made. Parties of national minorities, such as the **South Schleswig Voters' Association** of the Danish minority and the Frisians, are exempt from the hurdle. In 2025 the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance missed getting in by a very narrow margin with 4.981 per cent.

In Germany there is no threshold for elections to the European Parliament. In 2014 the Federal Constitutional Court declared the three per cent hurdle unconstitutional. It found that the parties' equal opportunities were violated, because the European Parliament does not have to support a government. That is why even very small parties from Germany enter the European Parliament. Other countries have their own rules for European elections.

In **Israel** the hurdle was raised step by step, most recently in 2014 from 2 to 3.25 per cent. Even so, more than ten parties usually sit in the Knesset, the Israeli parliament. **Turkey** had a hurdle of 10 per cent for decades, one of the highest in Europe. In 2022 it was lowered to 7 per cent. A calculation shows the effect: if parties below the hurdle together receive 15 per cent, a party with 42.5 per cent of the votes gets half of the seats, because 42.5 divided by 85 gives 0.5.

In the **National Council elections** there is no threshold set by law. But each canton is a separate constituency with a fixed number of seats. In small cantons only a few seats are shared out. A list there needs a high share of the votes to win a seat at all. This is called a **natural** or **de facto hurdle**.

gewusst: Although Israel has an electoral threshold, there are often more than ten parties in the Knesset.
In cantons with only one National Council seat, the person with the most votes simply wins.

teile.einleitung: Criminal law sets out which acts are forbidden and what punishment they can bring. In Switzerland the most important rules are in the Swiss Criminal Code. The state prosecutes and punishes such acts.
wichtigste: Criminal law says which acts the state punishes.
The Swiss Criminal Code has applied since 1 January 1942.
Before that, each canton had its own criminal law.
Offences prosecuted on complaint are only pursued if the injured person files a complaint.
Offences prosecuted ex officio are pursued by the authorities on their own initiative.
Monetary penalties are calculated in daily rates.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss Criminal Code**, StGB for short, was passed in **1937**. It came into force on **1 January 1942**. Before that, each **canton** had its own criminal law. Since then the same rules about what is a crime have applied throughout Switzerland.

Criminal law is meant to **protect** people and their property. It describes precisely which behaviour is forbidden. An important principle is: **no punishment without law**. So you may only be punished if the act was already set out in law as a crime beforehand. Until there is a verdict, every accused person is considered **innocent**.

With an **offence prosecuted on complaint**, the injured person must file a **criminal complaint**, for example in the case of simple damage to property. Without a complaint the act is not pursued. With an **offence prosecuted ex officio**, the police and the public prosecutor's office must act as soon as they learn about it. This applies to serious acts such as **robbery**. No complaint is needed for this.

The law has different penalties, such as the **fine**, the **monetary penalty** and the **prison sentence**. The monetary penalty is calculated in **daily rates**. The court decides the number of daily rates according to how serious the act is. The amount of a daily rate depends on **income**. That way the penalty hits poor and rich people about equally hard.
Children and young people have their own **juvenile criminal law**. It relies above all on **education** and protection. Young people should learn to take responsibility and find a good path again.

gewusst: In Switzerland children under 10 cannot be punished.
Since 2011 a uniform Criminal Procedure Code has applied throughout Switzerland, setting out how criminal proceedings work.

teile.einleitung: In the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, people vote in the open air at the Landsgemeinde. There, men may show a side arm instead of a paper identity card. A side arm is a bladed weapon that you wear at your side, for example a sword or a sabre.
wichtigste: In Appenzell Innerrhoden the side arm counts as a voting card for men.
Swords, sabres and bayonets count as side arms.
A sword of this kind has a long, narrow blade.
Many swords are passed down in the family.
Women, and men too, can show the paper voting card.

abschnitte.text: A **side arm** is not a firearm but a **bladed weapon**. You wear it in a sheath on your belt at the hip, that is, at your side. A **sword** of this kind has a long, narrow metal blade. The **sabre** and the **bayonet** also count. A bayonet is a blade that can also be fixed onto a rifle.

abschnitte.titel: The voting card at the Landsgemeinde
abschnitte.text: At the **Landsgemeinde** in Appenzell Innerrhoden, the people entitled to vote gather in a square and vote by raising their hands. There, men may show their side arm as a **voting card**. Women show the paper voting card. Men may also use this card. Many swords are passed on by a father or grandfather and are a valuable **heirloom**.

In the past, it was mainly the men who **defended** the land in war who were allowed to have a say. The weapon therefore showed that someone was a full citizen and could take part in decisions. Today the side arm is above all a **tradition**. It is a reminder of the long history of the Landsgemeinde.

gewusst: In Appenzell Innerrhoden an old family sword can serve as a card for voting.
Despite its German name, which contains the word for “gun”, the side arm is not a firearm but a blade.

teile.einleitung: Compulsory voting means that you have to take part in votes and elections. In Switzerland there is no general duty to vote; voting is voluntary. One exception with a long history is the canton of Schaffhausen, where compulsory voting still applies today.
wichtigste: Compulsory voting means that you have to vote and elect.
In Switzerland voting is voluntary as a rule.
The canton of Schaffhausen has compulsory voting with a long tradition.
Anyone there who does not vote without a good reason has to pay a small fine.
In the past other cantons also had compulsory voting.
Countries such as Belgium, Australia and Brazil have compulsory voting in elections.

abschnitte.text: With **compulsory voting**, all voters must take part in votes and elections. You do not have to say yes or no; you may also hand in a blank paper. All that matters is that you take part. Anyone who stays away without an excuse is punished, usually with a small fine.

In Switzerland taking part in federal votes is **voluntary**. Nobody is punished for not voting. That is why **turnout** is often only about 40 to 50 per cent. But on important or controversial topics, a lot more people go to the ballot box.

In the canton of **Schaffhausen**, compulsory voting has applied since the 19th century. Anyone who does not vote and has no reason for it has to pay a fine of 6 francs. This duty applies to votes and elections in the canton and at federal level too. That is why turnout in Schaffhausen is usually higher than in the rest of Switzerland.

In the past, several cantons had compulsory voting, for example at the Landsgemeinden. Anyone who did not turn up could be punished. Over time almost all cantons abolished this duty again. Only Schaffhausen has kept it to this day.

Around the world some countries have **compulsory voting in elections**, such as Belgium, Luxembourg, Australia and Brazil. Supporters say that this way everyone's opinion is counted. Opponents think that freedom also includes not voting. This question is discussed again and again in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The duty to take part in votes and elections.
The share of voters who have voted.
A money penalty for breaking a rule in a small way.
A container into which you put your ballot paper.

gewusst: Because of compulsory voting, Schaffhausen often has the highest turnout of all cantons in federal votes.
The fine of 6 francs is so small that it is more about the signal than about the money.
Australia introduced compulsory voting as early as 1924.

teile.einleitung: Tax liability means that a person or company has to pay taxes. Anyone who lives or works in Switzerland is usually liable to pay tax. How much you pay depends on income, assets and where you live.
wichtigste: Anyone who lives in Switzerland is usually **liable to pay tax** here.
For taxes, what usually counts is where you live on **31 December**.
An apprentice's wage is taxed **to the apprentice themselves**.
With **tax progression**, the tax rate rises with income.
With **tax at source**, the tax is deducted directly from the wage.
Anyone who declares their assets correctly gets the **withholding tax** of 35 per cent back.
If you do not hand in a tax return, the tax office makes an assessment.

abschnitte.text: Anyone whose **place of residence** is in Switzerland is usually liable to pay tax here. What counts is your place of residence at the end of the tax period, that is, on **31 December**. If you move to another canton in the autumn, you pay the taxes for the whole year in the new canton. Because each canton sets its own tax rates, you pay different amounts depending on the canton. In most cantons, members of a recognised **national church** also pay a **church tax**.

The **earned income** of minors is taxed separately from their parents. A 16-year-old apprentice therefore pays tax on their wage themselves. Depending on the canton and the size of the wage, they fill in their own **tax return**. At the latest from the year in which you turn 18, you usually have to hand in a tax return yourself. In it you state your income and assets.

With **tax progression** you pay a higher percentage on higher incomes. So people who earn little pay not only fewer francs but also a smaller share. This way people with a lot of income contribute more to the state's tasks. VAT affects everyone too: if a toy costs 100 francs without tax, it costs **108.10 francs** with 8.1 per cent VAT. But this tax is the same for everyone, no matter how much you earn.

With **tax at source**, the employer deducts the tax directly from the wage. It applies mainly to foreign employees without a settlement permit, that is, without a C permit. The **withholding tax** is 35 per cent and is deducted, for example, from interest on savings accounts. Anyone who declares their savings correctly in their tax return gets it back. So it pays to be honest.

abschnitte.titel: When the tax return is missing
abschnitte.text: Anyone who does not hand in their tax return despite a reminder is assessed **at the tax office's discretion**. This means the tax office estimates income and assets itself. A **fine** can also be imposed. The estimate often turns out rather high. That is why it is wiser to hand in your tax return on time.

gewusst: The withholding tax is so high so that it pays to declare your savings honestly.
If you move on 31 December, you pay the whole year's taxes at your new place of residence.

teile.einleitung: Many countries in the world are republics, including Switzerland. In a republic there is no king or queen who inherits their office. Instead, the head of state is chosen for a certain period of time.
wichtigste: The word republic comes from the Latin “res publica”, public affair.
In a republic, the head of state is chosen for a limited time and does not inherit the office.
Switzerland is a republic.
Venice was a republic for over a thousand years, until Napoleon ended it in 1797.
Austria became a republic in 1918, and Italy chose to become one in a referendum in 1946.
From 1798 to 1803, the Helvetic Republic existed on the territory of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The word **republic** comes from the Latin **“res publica”**. This means **“public affair”**: the state should be a matter for everyone and not belong to a single family. The opposite is a **monarchy**, in which a king, queen or prince usually inherits the office. In a republic, the **head of state is chosen for a limited time**. But a republic is not automatically a democracy; some dictatorships also call themselves republics.

**Switzerland** is a republic and a federal state. There is no head of state in the narrow sense: this role is taken on by the **Federal Council** as a body of seven members. The President of the Confederation changes every year. From **1798 to 1803**, the **Helvetic Republic** existed on the territory of Switzerland. It was founded under the influence of France and was a unitary state.

Ancient **Rome** already had a republic before the emperors took power. One of the most famous republics was **Venice**. The city by the sea was a powerful republic for over **a thousand years** and was led by an elected Doge. In **1797**, **Napoleon** ended the Republic of Venice. In France itself, the **First Republic** was proclaimed in **1792** after the monarchy had been overthrown.

Switzerland's neighbours also became republics. **Austria** became a republic in **1918** after the end of the **Habsburg monarchy**. In the same year the monarchy also ended in Germany. In **1946**, **Italy** decided in a **referendum** that it no longer wanted to be a monarchy but a republic. Liechtenstein, on the other hand, is still a principality today, in other words a monarchy.

gewusst: The Republic of San Marino in Italy is considered one of the oldest republics in the world that still exists.
France counts its republics: since 1958 the Fifth Republic has been in place.

teile.einleitung: The tax multiplier (in German “Steuerfuss”) decides how much tax you pay to your municipality or canton. It is a percentage of what is called the simple tax. Each municipality sets its own tax multiplier every year.
wichtigste: The **tax multiplier** is a percentage of the **simple tax**.
The simple tax comes from the cantonal tax scale.
With a tax multiplier of **100 per cent** you pay exactly the simple tax.
The tax multiplier is set **every year**, usually together with the budget.
In municipalities without a parliament, the **municipal assembly** decides.
It applies mainly to income tax and wealth tax.

abschnitte.text: First the tax office works out the **simple tax** from income and assets. For this, the canton's tax scale applies. Then the simple tax is multiplied by the **tax multiplier**. With a tax multiplier of 100 per cent you pay exactly the simple tax. If it is higher, you pay more; if it is lower, you pay less.

If the simple tax is 2000 francs and the tax multiplier is 110 per cent, you calculate 2000 times 1.1. That gives **2200 francs** of municipal tax. With 3000 francs of simple tax and a tax multiplier of 95 per cent, you calculate 3000 times 0.95, so **2850 francs**. If a municipality raises the tax multiplier from 100 to 120 per cent, the tax on 1500 francs of simple tax goes up by **300 francs**. So just a few percentage points make a noticeable amount of money.

In municipalities without a parliament, the voters set the tax multiplier at the **municipal assembly**. In municipalities with a parliament, the **parliament** usually does this. The cantons also set their own tax multiplier. The tax multiplier is decided **every year**, usually together with the **budget**. That way the canton and the municipality can respond to their financial situation.

The tax multiplier applies mainly to **income tax** and **wealth tax**. VAT and customs duties, on the other hand, belong to the Confederation. Because each municipality decides for itself, tax multipliers are very different. Anyone who lives in a municipality with a low tax multiplier pays less tax on the same income. Municipalities with many tasks or little income often need a higher tax multiplier.

gewusst: With a tax multiplier of 100 per cent, the simple tax and the municipal tax are exactly the same.
Two neighbouring municipalities can have very different tax multipliers.

teile.einleitung: Subsidiarity means that a task should be carried out at the lowest sensible level. What the municipality can solve well itself should not be done by the canton, and what the canton can solve should not be done by the Confederation. This principle is an important part of how the Swiss state is built.
wichtigste: Subsidiarity means that tasks are carried out at the lowest sensible level.
In Switzerland there are three levels: municipality, canton and Confederation.
The higher level only helps if the lower one cannot manage a task alone.
The principle of subsidiarity has been in the Federal Constitution since 2008.
The word comes from the Latin “subsidium” and means help.
The European Union also has the principle of subsidiarity.

abschnitte.text: The word **subsidiarity** comes from the Latin “subsidium”, which means help or support. The idea is that the larger community should only help when the smaller one cannot carry out a task itself. So first it is up to the people themselves, the family and the municipality. Only after that come the canton and the Confederation.

Switzerland has three **levels of the state**: about 2100 municipalities, 26 cantons and the Confederation. The municipalities look after things such as nursery schools, primary schools, rubbish and local roads. The cantons are responsible, among other things, for the police, hospitals and grammar schools. The Confederation governs what has to be the same for the whole country, such as the army, foreign policy and money.

Since 2008 the principle has been set out expressly in Article 5a of the **Federal Constitution**. It says that the principle of subsidiarity must be respected when state tasks are assigned and carried out. It was added with the reform of financial equalisation between the Confederation and the cantons. But the principle had been practised in Switzerland for much longer.

The municipality often knows the local problems better than the Confederation in Bern. Solutions can therefore be better suited to the people. Citizens can have a say more closely, for example at the **municipal assembly**. This also leads to differences between cantons, for example in school holidays or taxes.

The term became well known especially through Catholic **social teaching**, above all through a papal letter from 1931. Later the European Union also took it into its treaties. There, the EU should only act if the member states cannot achieve a goal well enough on their own. Germany and Austria also have the principle in how their states are built.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tasks are carried out as far down as possible.
Municipality, canton or Confederation.
Dividing power between the federal level and the member states.
Rich cantons and the Confederation help poorer cantons with money.

gewusst: Because the cantons are responsible for schools, the summer holidays in Switzerland do not start on the same day everywhere.
Most of the taxes that Swiss people pay go to the canton and the municipality, not to the Confederation.
The number of municipalities falls every year because of mergers.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss cross is a white cross on a red background. It is the best-known symbol of Switzerland and appears on the flag, on the passport and on many products. The Swiss flag has a special shape: it is square.
wichtigste: The Swiss cross is white and stands free on a red background.
On land the Swiss flag is square.
Only Switzerland and Vatican City have a square flag.
On ships the Swiss flag is rectangular.
The symbol of the Red Cross is the Swiss flag with the colours swapped.
On 1 August many people hang out the flag.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss flag is **square**, which means it is as high as it is wide. That is very rare for national flags. Only **Vatican City** also has a square flag. The white cross stands **free in the middle** and does not touch the edge. On **ships**, however, a rectangular Swiss flag flies, as is usual everywhere on the water.

On **1 August** Switzerland celebrates its national day. Many people then hang the flag on their house or balcony. That way they show they are joining in the celebrations. On this day you also often see the Swiss cross on paper lanterns, napkins and cakes.

Many products carry the Swiss cross. It shows that they come **from Switzerland**. The cross is seen as a sign of quality. That is why there are rules: not every product may simply carry the cross; it must really come largely from Switzerland.

The **Red Cross** is an aid organisation that was founded in Switzerland. It was **Henry Dunant** from Geneva who inspired its founding. For this he received the first **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1901. In honour of Switzerland, its flag with the **colours swapped** was chosen as the symbol: a red cross on a white background.

gewusst: In the whole world only two countries have a square flag: Switzerland and Vatican City.
The symbol of the Red Cross is a reversed Swiss flag.

teile.einleitung: At the Landsgemeinde, the open-air cantonal assembly, voters vote in the open air. They stand in a marked-off area called the ring. Landsgemeinden still exist today in the cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
wichtigste: The ring is the area where voters stand at the Landsgemeinde.
Spectators without the right to vote stay outside the ring.
The Landsgemeinde takes place in the open air.
Most voters follow it standing up.
During the Landsgemeinde, the government stands on a platform.
In Glarus, every voter in the ring may speak for themselves.

abschnitte.text: The **Landsgemeinde** is an assembly of all the voters of a canton. It takes place **in the open air** on a large square. The voters stand in a marked-off area, the **ring**. Most follow the Landsgemeinde **standing up**, often for several hours. Voting is done by a show of hands. Spectators who are not allowed to vote stay **outside the ring**.

During the Landsgemeinde, the **government** stands on a **platform** in the ring. From there the Landammann leads the assembly. For each vote, he estimates which side has more hands. In **Glarus**, **every voter** in the ring may **speak for themselves** about an item of business. They can even propose changes. To do this, they step up to the speaker's platform.

The Glarus Landsgemeinde takes place every May in the cantonal capital, Glarus. In Glarus you can vote **from the age of 16**. In the local dialect, the voters in the ring are called the **“Mitlandlüüt”**. Besides the voters, **guests of honour** may also enter the ring, for example members of the Federal Council or guests from abroad. Glarus **schoolchildren** who are not allowed to vote may follow the Landsgemeinde from close up: they stand **next to the speaker's platform**.

In **Appenzell Innerrhoden**, the Landsgemeinde takes place in April in the village of Appenzell. There, too, the voters stand in the ring on the Landsgemeinde square. Traditionally, many men carry a sword or a bayonet. In the past this was proof that you had the right to vote. Since 1991, women have also been allowed to vote at the Innerrhoden Landsgemeinde.

gewusst: In the past there were Landsgemeinden in more cantons, for example in Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Obwalden and Nidwalden, but they were abolished.
At the Landsgemeinde, the hands are not counted during votes but estimated.

teile.einleitung: The treaty referendum is a people's right in Switzerland that lets the people vote on international treaties. Switzerland concludes such treaties with other countries or international organisations. For particularly important treaties, the people have the last word under certain conditions.
wichtigste: With the treaty referendum, the people can vote on international treaties.
A treaty is an agreement between states.
There is a mandatory and an optional treaty referendum.
When joining certain organisations, the people must always vote.
An optional treaty referendum needs 50,000 signatures in 100 days or eight cantons.
The treaty referendum has existed since 1921.

abschnitte.text: A **treaty** is a binding agreement between two or more states. It can be about trade, transport, taxes, environmental protection or police cooperation, for example. For Switzerland, the Federal Council signs such treaties. Important treaties must then be approved by parliament.

For particularly important treaties the people must always vote; this is the **mandatory** treaty referendum. It applies to joining organisations for collective security or supranational communities. Then a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons are needed. A well-known example is the vote on the European Economic Area, **EEA** for short, in 1992, which the people narrowly rejected.

Other important treaties are subject to the **optional** referendum. These include treaties that are unlimited in time and cannot be terminated, that provide for joining an international organisation or that contain important legal rules. Anyone who wants a vote must collect 50,000 signatures in 100 days, or eight cantons must call for it. Then a majority of the people is enough.

The treaty referendum was introduced in 1921, at first only for very long treaties. It was later extended in 1977 and 2003. This was a response to the fact that more and more important rules are set out in international treaties. That way **direct democracy** is kept in foreign policy too.

In 2005 the people voted on the **Schengen** and Dublin agreements and accepted them. There was also a vote on the Bilateral Agreements with the European Union in 2000. Such votes are often fiercely debated. They show how important the relationship with the EU is for Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A binding agreement between states.
Standing above the individual states, like the European Union.
States protect themselves together, for example in an alliance.
Parliament's agreement to a treaty.

gewusst: The EEA was rejected in 1992 by a very narrow margin, with about 50.3 per cent voting no.
Switzerland has concluded several thousand treaties with other states, but only a few of them were put to a vote.

teile.einleitung: Respect means treating other people with care and kindness. If you show respect, you take others seriously and respect their feelings and belongings. Respect makes living together in the family, at school and in the village much more pleasant.
wichtigste: If someone gives you something, you say “thank you”.
You use “please” to ask politely.
Respectful people listen when someone is speaking.
In German-speaking Switzerland, you greet an adult you do not know with “Grüezi”.
You knock before entering someone else's room.
You treat other people's belongings carefully.

abschnitte.text: Two small words are very important: **please** and **thank you**. You use “please” to ask **politely**, for example: “Could you please pass me the pencil?” When someone gives you something or helps you, you say **“thank you”**. That way you show that you value the help. These words cost nothing, but they make others happy.

In **German-speaking Switzerland**, you politely greet an adult you do not know with **“Grüezi”**. Friends and family are often greeted with “Hoi” or “Sali”. In French-speaking Switzerland people say “Bonjour”, and in Ticino “Buongiorno”. You also show respect by **listening** while someone is talking to you. You look at the person and do not interrupt them.

Before you go into someone else's room, you **knock** and wait for an answer. That way you respect other people's privacy. You treat **other children's belongings** **carefully**, even if you are only borrowing them. If an older person has no seat on a full bus, you **offer them your seat**. The same applies to people on crutches or carrying a small child.

Not everyone is equally good at everything. If another child cannot do something, it is respectful to **help** them instead of laughing at them. Respect also means listening to other opinions, even if you do not agree. Every person is different, and everyone has the same **dignity**. If you are respectful yourself, others usually treat you with respect too.

gewusst: The word respect comes from the Latin “respectus”, which means consideration or looking back.
In Switzerland, people on mountain footpaths often greet each other, even if they do not know each other.

teile.einleitung: The Rütli is a meadow high above Lake Uri. According to legend, men from Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden swore an alliance here. That is why the Rütli is regarded as a special place in Swiss history.
wichtigste: The Rütli lies on Lake Uri in the municipality of Seelisberg in the canton of Uri.
The meadow covers about 6 hectares, as much as several football pitches.
In 1859, the Swiss Society for the Common Good collected money from the public to buy the Rütli.
Since 1860 the Rütli has belonged to the Swiss Confederation.
The easiest way to reach the Rütli is by boat, for example from Brunnen.
In 1940, General Henri Guisan held the Rütli Report here.
Every year on 1 August, a national day celebration takes place on the Rütli.

abschnitte.titel: Location and how to get there
abschnitte.text: The Rütli lies on the shore of **Lake Uri**, part of Lake Lucerne. It belongs to the municipality of **Seelisberg** in the canton of Uri. From Seelisberg you can walk down in about an hour. But the easiest way is by **boat**; the trip from Brunnen takes only about ten minutes.

In the 19th century, a hotel was going to be built on the Rütli. Many people wanted to prevent this. In 1859 the **Swiss Society for the Common Good** collected money from the public and bought the meadow. In 1860 it gave the Rütli to the **Swiss Confederation**. It may never be sold and so belongs to the whole of Switzerland.

On **25 July 1940**, during the Second World War, **General Henri Guisan** called the army's senior officers together on the Rütli. This is known as the **Rütli Report**. Guisan wanted to show that Switzerland intended to defend itself. The place was chosen deliberately because it stands for freedom and unity.

On **1 August**, Swiss National Day, a celebration takes place on the Rütli every year. Many guests come by boat. For the 700th anniversary in 1991, the **Swiss Path** was created around Lake Uri. The Rütli is one of its highlights.

gewusst: On the Swiss Path, each canton has its own section, longer or shorter depending on its population.
There is no road for cars on the Rütli.

teile.einleitung: The presumption of innocence is an important principle under the rule of law. Anyone accused of a crime is considered innocent until a court has convicted them with a final judgement.
wichtigste: Every person is considered innocent until they are convicted with a final judgement.
In Switzerland the presumption of innocence is set out in Article 32 of the Federal Constitution.
Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights also protects it.
The authorities must prove guilt; the accused person does not have to prove their innocence.
“In dubio pro reo” means: when in doubt, in favour of the accused.
Even someone in pre-trial detention is still considered innocent.

abschnitte.text: If someone is suspected of having committed a crime, that is not yet proof. The person is considered **innocent** until a court convicts them with a **final** judgement. Final means that the judgement can no longer be challenged. This is the case when the time limit for an appeal has run out or the highest court has decided. In this way the principle protects everyone from hasty punishment.

In Switzerland the presumption of innocence is set out in **Article 32 of the Federal Constitution**. The **Criminal Procedure Code** also names this principle. On top of that comes **Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights**, by which Switzerland is bound. It guarantees a fair trial. The UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights also contains the presumption of innocence.

The **criminal prosecution authorities**, that is, the police and the public prosecutor's office, must prove guilt. The accused person does not have to prove their innocence. Closely linked to this is the Latin phrase **“in dubio pro reo”**. It means: when in doubt, in favour of the accused. If real doubts about guilt remain, the court must acquit the person.

Sometimes someone is held in **pre-trial detention** before the verdict. This is not a punishment, but is meant, for example, to prevent escape or the covering up of evidence. The person is therefore still considered innocent. Newspapers and news reports also respect the principle. They write about an **“alleged” offender** as long as there is only a suspicion.

gewusst: The presumption of innocence applies only to the state and the court, but the media should still not prejudge anyone.
The phrase “in dubio pro reo” comes from Latin and is still used in courts today.

teile.einleitung: In ancient Rome, the Senate was a very important assembly. In the Roman Republic it advised the officials and had great influence on politics. We find many ideas from that time in today's states.
wichtigste: According to tradition, the Roman Republic was founded in 509 BC.
The word “senate” comes from the Latin “senex”, old man.
Senators usually sat in the Senate for life.
At the head of the republic were two consuls each year.
Tribunes of the people protected the ordinary citizens, the plebeians.
In an emergency, a dictator could rule for a maximum of six months.
Julius Caesar was murdered by senators in 44 BC.

abschnitte.text: The word senate comes from the Latin **senex**, which means old man. So originally the Senate was a **council of elders**. Later it was made up mainly of former officials. As a rule they remained members **for life**. The Senate advised the officials and had a strong say over money, war and foreign policy.

At first Rome was ruled by kings. According to legend, in **509 BC** the Romans drove out their last king, **Tarquinius Superbus**. After that the **republic** was created. The word means roughly “the public affair”. Power was now to be shared among several people and assemblies.

Every year **two consuls** were elected. They could keep a check on each other, so that nobody became too powerful. The **tribunes of the people** protected the plebeians and could stop decisions with their **veto**. In a great emergency, a **dictator** was allowed to rule, but for a maximum of six months.

In the first century BC, individual generals became more and more powerful. **Julius Caesar** finally had himself made dictator for life and in doing so broke the old rules. On the **Ides of March 44 BC**, senators killed him during a meeting because they saw the republic under threat. Shortly afterwards the age of the emperors began, and the Senate lost much of its power.

gewusst: The abbreviation SPQR means “the Senate and People of Rome” and appeared on military standards and buildings.
Today, too, chambers of parliament in some countries are called the Senate, for example in the USA and Italy.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is a small country in the middle of Europe, known for its mountains, its four national languages and its direct democracy. It is a federal state made up of 26 cantons. Its federal city is Bern, and the people may decide directly on many questions.
wichtigste: Switzerland is a federal state made up of 26 cantons.
The federal city is Bern, where parliament meets in the Federal Palace.
Parliament has two chambers: the National Council and the Council of States.
The government is the Federal Council, with seven members.
Swiss National Day is on 1 August.
The currency is the Swiss franc.
There are four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland lies in Central Europe and borders Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein. It covers about 41,000 square kilometres. Large parts of the country belong to the **Alps**, and there are also the Central Plateau and the Jura. The highest mountain is the Dufourspitze, at 4,634 metres.

The year of foundation is considered to be 1291, when Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promised each other help according to the **Federal Charter**. Over the centuries, other places joined. In 1848, with a new constitution, Switzerland became a modern **federal state**. The youngest canton is Jura, which was created in 1979.

In Bern stands the **Federal Palace**, where parliament meets. It consists of the National Council, with 200 members, and the Council of States, with 46 members. The government is the Federal Council, with seven members. Through popular initiatives and referendums, the people can vote directly on issues.

About 9 million people live in Switzerland (as of 2024). Switzerland has four **national languages**: German, French, Italian and Romansh. Most people speak German, often Swiss German in everyday life. About a quarter of the population does not have a Swiss passport.

People pay with the **franc**, abbreviated CHF. Important industries are banking and insurance, pharmaceuticals, mechanical engineering, watches and tourism. Swiss chocolate and cheese are also famous. Switzerland is one of the richest countries in the world.

On 1 August, Switzerland celebrates its National Day with bonfires on hilltops, paper lanterns and fireworks. The flag shows a white cross on a red background and is square. Switzerland has long been **neutral** and does not fight in any wars. Many international organisations have their headquarters in Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state made up of member states, which in Switzerland are the cantons.
The seat of government and parliament, which in Switzerland is Bern.
The country does not fight on either side in any war.
One of the four official languages of Switzerland.

gewusst: Officially, Switzerland has no capital city; Bern is called the “federal city”.
The abbreviation CH stands for the Latin name Confoederatio Helvetica.
Apart from the Vatican, Switzerland is the only country with a square national flag.

teile.einleitung: For many children, the school trip is a highlight of the school year. The whole class goes on an outing together. Often the class is even allowed to help decide where to go.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, a class usually goes on a school trip once a year.
Often they go to the mountains, a lake or a zoo.
Many classes travel by train.
The destination must be reachable in one day and safe.
In a vote, you first collect suggestions.
The destination with the most votes wins.

abschnitte.text: The **school trip** is an outing with the whole class. In Switzerland it usually takes place **once a year**. Because Switzerland has a dense **rail network**, many classes travel by **train**. Buses and boats are popular too. In the evening, everyone comes back tired but happy.

A destination must be reachable **in one day**. A **zoo**, a mountain or a lake nearby are good choices. Countries such as Australia or Japan are much too far away for this. Above all, the teacher makes sure the destination is **safe**. The children's safety is the most important thing.

Sometimes the class may **vote** on the destination. First you collect **suggestions**, and everyone may say their ideas. Then each child votes, and **every vote counts the same**. With 6 votes for the swimming pool, 10 for a hike and 4 for a museum, the hike wins because it has the **most votes**. That way you learn on a small scale how **democracy** works.

For a **hike**, you pack a **rucksack with a packed lunch**. This includes food and above all enough to drink. Good shoes and a raincoat are important too. In many areas there are **fire pits** along the way where you can grill a sausage.

gewusst: In Switzerland there are cheap tickets for trains and boats for school classes.
For many children in Switzerland, grilling sausages at a fire pit is part of a proper school trip.

teile.einleitung: After an election, all the votes have to be counted precisely. Only then is it clear who has been elected. In a National Council election this is a lot of work, because there are many names and lists.
wichtigste: In the National Council election the counting happens on **election Sunday**.
Counting an election takes longer than counting a vote on an issue.
The **computer** helps to add up the votes.
The votes of registered **Swiss citizens abroad** are counted too.
Ballot papers with insults are **invalid**.
The final result shows how many **seats** each party gets.

abschnitte.text: The National Council is elected every four years in October. Many voters vote by post; others go to the ballot box on Sunday. After the ballot boxes close on **election Sunday**, the counting begins. The **polling stations' electoral offices** in the municipalities are responsible for it. Many results are already available in the evening.

abschnitte.titel: Many names, a lot of work
abschnitte.text: In a vote on an issue you only count yes and no. A National Council election is more complicated. You choose a **list**, but you can cross out names, add names from other lists (**panachage**) or write a name twice (**cumulation**). All these votes for people and lists have to be recorded. That is why counting an election takes longer.

The votes on the ballot papers are recorded and then added up by **computer**. This makes the results come faster. The municipalities report their figures to the canton. The votes of **Swiss citizens living abroad** who have registered are also counted in their voting canton. In the end, a result is worked out for each canton.

Not every ballot paper counts. A paper with **defamatory remarks**, that is, insults, is **invalid**. Papers that have not been filled in correctly can also be invalid. Invalid papers are not taken into account in the count. That is why it pays to fill in your ballot paper carefully.

On election evening, **television**, **radio** and the **internet** report on the results live. The Confederation and the cantons also publish the figures online. After the count it is clear how many **seats** each party gets in each canton. After that, it is decided which people on the lists are elected. These are the ones with the most personal votes on their list.

gewusst: In the National Council election you can write the same name twice on the ballot paper; this is called cumulation.
The seats are first shared out among the lists and only after that among the people.

teile.einleitung: The debt brake is a rule in the Federal Constitution. It is meant to prevent the Confederation from permanently spending more money than it takes in. In bad times it allows a small deficit; in good times it requires a surplus.
wichtigste: The people and the cantons accepted the debt brake on 2 December 2001.
The Confederation has applied it since 2003.
Over an economic cycle, spending may not be higher than income.
In a crisis a limited deficit is allowed; in good years a surplus is needed.
Deviations are recorded in the compensation account.
Extraordinary spending needs a qualified majority in both chambers.
During the coronavirus pandemic, the Confederation used this exception rule.

abschnitte.text: In the **1990s**, the Confederation's debts rose sharply. Many people wanted to stop this from going on and on. On **2 December 2001**, the people and the cantons approved the **debt brake** by a large majority. It was applied from **2003**. Since then, the Confederation's debt ratio has fallen.

Over an **economic cycle**, the Confederation may not spend more than it takes in. An economic cycle is the up and down of the economy over several years. In an **economic crisis**, income falls, so a **limited deficit** is allowed. When the economy is doing very well, the Confederation must achieve a **surplus**. That way good and bad years balance each other out.

If the Confederation spends more or less than the rule allows, the difference is recorded in the **compensation account**. This account, so to speak, remembers whether the Confederation has spent too much or too little. **Shortfalls** must be made up again in later years. That way a gap cannot build up unnoticed.

In serious crises or natural disasters, **extraordinary spending** is possible. For this a **qualified majority** is needed: the majority of all members of both chambers must agree, not just of those present. From 2020, during the **coronavirus pandemic**, the Confederation spent billions on short-time working and loans to companies. This spending was recorded as extraordinary. How strict the debt brake should be is discussed again and again in politics.

gewusst: The debt brake is in the Federal Constitution, so it can only be changed by a popular vote.
Many cantons also have their own rules that limit their debts.

teile.einleitung: The right to vote is the right to help decide in elections and votes. In Switzerland all Swiss citizens who are at least 18 years old have it. They are called voters.
wichtigste: With the right to vote, you can elect and vote.
Swiss citizens who are of age are entitled to vote.
Since 1991 the federal voting age has been 18.
Women have only had the right to vote at federal level since 1971.
The voting card shows that you are allowed to vote.
In the canton of Glarus you can vote from the age of 16.
Swiss citizens living abroad also have the right to vote at federal level.

abschnitte.titel: What is the right to vote?
abschnitte.text: The **right to vote** is one of the political rights. Anyone who has it may say yes or no in votes and choose people in elections. They may also sign popular initiatives and referendums. Being able to be elected to an office yourself is called the **right to stand for election**, which is closely linked to it.

At federal level, all **voters** who have Swiss citizenship and are 18 years old take part. Foreign residents may not vote at federal level. But in some cantons, such as Neuchâtel and Jura, they may have a say in the municipality. Swiss citizens who live abroad may also take part in federal votes.

Before every vote you receive the papers at home by post. They include the **voting card**, a paper that shows that you are allowed to vote. You have to sign it and hand it in together with the ballot paper. This prevents anyone from voting more than once.

For a long time only men were allowed to vote in Switzerland. Only on 7 February 1971 did the men accept **votes for women** at federal level. The last canton was Appenzell Innerrhoden, which had to introduce it in 1990 on the orders of the Federal Supreme Court. This made Switzerland one of the last countries in Europe.

Until 1991 the federal voting age was 20. Then the people agreed to lower it to **18**. In 2007 the canton of Glarus became the only canton to introduce a voting age of 16 for cantonal and municipal votes. There were votes on this in other cantons, but the proposals were mostly rejected.

begriffe.erklaerung: People who are allowed to help make political decisions.
A paper that shows that you are allowed to vote.
Nationality, that is, the Swiss passport.
Adult in the eyes of the law; in Switzerland from 18.

gewusst: In Switzerland over 5 million people are entitled to vote (as of 2024).
In the first vote in 1959, the men still clearly rejected votes for women.
Most voters today vote by post and no longer go to the polling station at all.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who wants to call a referendum against a new federal law does not have unlimited time. The signatures must be collected within a fixed period, the referendum period. It lasts 100 days.
wichtigste: The referendum period lasts 100 days from the official publication of the law.
Before the revision of 1977, it lasted 90 days.
During this time, 50,000 valid signatures are needed.
The signatures, with certification of voting rights, must reach the Federal Chancellery in time.
Without a referendum, a law comes into force at the earliest once the 100 days are over.
The period is not extended even during the summer holidays.

abschnitte.text: When parliament has passed a new federal law, it is officially published in the **Federal Gazette**. From that day, the **referendum period** of **100 days** begins. An example: if a law is published on 1 October, the period ends in **January**. Before a revision in **1977**, the period was **90 days**. At the same time, the number of signatures needed was raised from 30,000 to 50,000.

A referendum needs **50,000 valid signatures**. Counting on about 14 weeks, that is on average **about 3,600 signatures a week**. A sample calculation: after 60 days a committee has 32,000 signatures. It still needs 18,000, and there are 40 days left. So it must collect on average **450 signatures a day**. Because some signatures are invalid, committees usually collect more than necessary.

The signatures first have to be checked by the municipalities. With a **certification of voting rights**, they confirm that the people are entitled to vote. Only then do the signatures count. By the end of the 100 days, the signatures with this certification must have reached the **Federal Chancellery**. That is why a committee must stop collecting in good time and hand everything in.

The referendum period is **fixed**: even summer holidays or public holidays do not extend it. For a **popular initiative** you need twice as many signatures, namely 100,000, but you have 18 months. Calculated per day, a referendum is therefore **harder to collect for**, because the period is much shorter. If no referendum is called, the law can come into force **at the earliest once the 100 days are over**.

gewusst: For some time now, there have been organisations that collect signatures for payment. This is controversial in Switzerland.
The Federal Chancellery checks every signature list before announcing whether a referendum has succeeded.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Assembly, that is, the National Council and the Council of States together, works in sessions. These are periods of a few weeks in which parliament sits in Bern. Each session has its fixed routine and its typical business.
wichtigste: The Federal Assembly is a militia parliament and therefore sits in sessions.
In the winter session after the elections, the whole Federal Council is elected.
In the summer session the state accounts are approved.
Tuesday afternoon is set aside for parliamentary group meetings.
On Mondays the National Council only starts at 2.30 pm.
The first session outside Bern took place in Geneva in 1993.

abschnitte.text: Most members of parliament have a **job** alongside their seat. That is why the Federal Assembly is called a **militia parliament**. For this reason it does not meet all year round, but only for a few weeks in **sessions**. In between, the **committees** work. There, smaller groups of members prepare the business.

On **Monday** the National Council only begins at **2.30 pm**, so that members from all over Switzerland can travel there. On the other days it starts at 8 am. **Tuesday afternoon** is kept free: then the **parliamentary groups**, that is, the groups of the parties, hold their discussions. When there is a lot of business, there is an **evening sitting** from 7 pm to 10 pm, usually on the Monday of the second week of the session.

Some business always comes in the same session. The **state accounts** for the previous year show how much money the Confederation took in and spent. They are approved in the **summer session** in June. The **budget** for the next year only comes in winter. After the National Council elections in October, the new legislative period begins with the **winter session**. There, in December, the United Federal Assembly elects the whole **Federal Council**.

Normally parliament sits in the Federal Palace in Bern. But the **autumn session of 1993** took place in **Geneva**, the first session outside Bern. Later, further sessions followed in other parts of the country. In May and June 2020 the chambers met on the **Bernexpo** grounds because of the **COVID-19 pandemic**, because distances could not be kept in the Federal Palace.

gewusst: On Monday the National Council only starts in the afternoon, so that everyone can travel to Bern in time.
The whole Federal Council is always re-elected in December after the National Council elections.

teile.einleitung: The Sonderbund War of 1847 was the last war on Swiss soil. Liberal and Catholic-conservative cantons argued about how Switzerland should be organised. After the war, the modern federal state was created in 1848.
wichtigste: In 1845 seven Catholic-conservative cantons founded the **Sonderbund**.
Inviting the Jesuits to Lucerne made the dispute worse.
On 4 November 1847 the Diet decided to dissolve the Sonderbund by force of arms.
General **Guillaume-Henri Dufour** led the federal troops.
The battle of Gisikon on 23 November 1847 was decisive.
Valais was the last canton to surrender, on 29 November 1847.
The war lasted only a few weeks.

abschnitte.text: In the first half of the 19th century, Switzerland was a loose league of cantons, governed by the Federal Treaty of 1815. The **Liberals** wanted a strong federal state with shared laws. The **Catholic-conservative** cantons feared losing their independence and their faith. When Lucerne invited the **Jesuits** to its higher schools, the Liberals were outraged. This was followed by the Freischaren expeditions, that is, armed marches by volunteers against Lucerne.

On 11 December 1845 seven cantons joined together in Lucerne to form a protective alliance: Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug, Fribourg and Valais. Obwalden and Nidwalden were counted together as Unterwalden. The majority of the **Diet**, the assembly of the cantons, saw this as a breach of the Federal Treaty. The Sonderbund cantons hoped for help from **Austria**. But this help never came, because the conservative powers had problems of their own.

On 4 November 1847 the Diet in Bern decided to dissolve the Sonderbund by force of arms. General **Guillaume-Henri Dufour** led the federal troops and tried to avoid casualties as far as possible. The Sonderbund army was under the command of **Johann Ulrich von Salis-Soglio**, a Protestant from the Grisons. On 23 November the decision came at the battle of **Gisikon** on the River Reuss. The following day Lucerne was occupied.

After Lucerne, the other Sonderbund cantons gave up too. **Valais** was the last canton to surrender, on 29 November 1847. So the war lasted just under four weeks. Because Dufour acted quickly and carefully, there were comparatively few deaths. This helped the opponents to make peace again after the war.

After the Liberals' victory, the **Federal Constitution of 1848** was created. The loose confederation of states became a federal state with a Federal Council and a Federal Assembly. But the cantons kept many rights, which is called **federalism**. The Sonderbund War is regarded as the last war in Switzerland. To this day the Dufourspitze, the highest peak in Switzerland, is a reminder of the general.

gewusst: The Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif is named after General Dufour.
The commander-in-chief of the Catholic Sonderbund was himself a Protestant.
Only about half a year after the end of the war, the new Federal Constitution was accepted in 1848.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, all children must go to school. This is called compulsory schooling. Lessons at state schools are free and are organised by the cantons.
wichtigste: In most cantons, compulsory schooling lasts 11 years.
In most cantons it begins with kindergarten, at about the age of 4.
According to the Federal Constitution, lessons at state schools are free of charge.
Parents make sure their child goes to school.
The cantons are responsible for state schools.
In German-speaking Switzerland, Lehrplan 21 applies.
After compulsory school, a grammar school (Gymnasium), for example, is voluntary.

abschnitte.text: In most cantons, **compulsory schooling lasts 11 years**. This includes **2 years of kindergarten** and **9 years of school**. Children start kindergarten at about **4 years old**; what counts is a cut-off date in the summer. After that come **primary school** and **lower secondary school**.

In Switzerland, state schooling is **a matter for the cantons**. To make schools more alike, there is the **HarmoS agreement**, an agreement between cantons. Under it, primary level including kindergarten lasts 8 years, which means **6 years of primary school**. The 21 German-speaking and multilingual cantons have the common **Lehrplan 21** curriculum.

The **Federal Constitution** says that basic education at state schools is **free of charge**. Families pay no school fees; lessons are paid for with **tax money**. **Parents** are responsible for making sure their child attends school. If a child is ill, they may stay at home, and the parents **excuse** them to the school.

Compulsory schooling ends after **lower secondary school**. Then young people choose their next path. Many do an **apprenticeship**, while others attend a **grammar school** (Gymnasium) or a **specialised upper secondary school**. These courses are voluntary, but most young people go on to some form of education or training.

gewusst: Because the cantons are responsible, Switzerland actually has 26 different school systems.
Compulsory schooling applies to all children who live in Switzerland, whatever their nationality.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Trade Union Federation, SGB for short, is the largest umbrella organisation of employees in Switzerland. Many individual trade unions are joined together in it. It campaigns for good wages, good working conditions and secure pensions.
wichtigste: The SGB was founded in 1880.
It represents the interests of employees.
Its largest member union is Unia.
The VPOD organises staff in the public service.
In 2024 the people and the cantons accepted the initiative for a 13th AVS pension.
The minimum wage initiative was clearly rejected in 2014.
The SGB has traditionally been close to the SP.

abschnitte.text: A **trade union** is an association of employees. Together they carry more weight when they negotiate wages and working hours with employers. The SGB is an **umbrella organisation** of such unions. It was founded in **1880**, which makes it one of the oldest umbrella organisations in Switzerland. It represents its members' concerns to politicians and employers.

The largest trade union in Switzerland is **Unia**. It was formed in 2004 mainly from the GBI, the SMUV and the VHTL, that is, from unions for construction, industry and trade. Unia organises workers in construction, industry, trades and private services. The **VPOD** represents employees of the Confederation, the cantons, the municipalities and public companies. The **SEV** union mainly organises transport staff.

abschnitte.titel: Wins and defeats at the ballot box
abschnitte.text: The SGB also launches **popular initiatives**. In May 2014 the minimum wage initiative called for a national minimum wage of 22 francs an hour. About 76 per cent of voters rejected it. On **3 March 2024**, however, the people and the cantons accepted the initiative for a **13th AVS pension**. For an initiative from the trade unions, that was unusual.

Historically, the SGB has been close to **social democracy**. Many of its leading figures sit in the federal parliament for the **SP**. Its counterpart in the social partnership is the employers' associations. The trade unions often negotiate **collective labour agreements** with them, which set out wages and working hours.

gewusst: With the 13th AVS pension, the trade unions won a vote in 2024 that many people had not expected.
Unia was formed in 2004 from several unions and is now the largest in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Classified Compilation of Federal Legislation, SR for short, contains the federal law currently in force. Every law, ordinance and treaty has its own number in it. This way you find rules on the same topic together.
wichtigste: The SR is ordered by subject area.
The Federal Constitution has the number SR 101.
The Civil Code has SR 210, the Code of Obligations SR 220.
The digit 3 at the beginning stands for criminal law.
International treaties begin with a 0.
The SR also contains the cantonal constitutions.
The electronic version is updated continuously.

abschnitte.text: The **Classified Compilation** is a collection of the **federal law** in force. It contains laws, ordinances and **international treaties**. The **cantonal constitutions** are included too. **Court rulings**, on the other hand, are not part of it. Today the SR is found mainly in electronic form on the internet.

The acts are ordered by **subject area**. The first digit shows the area: **1** stands for state, people and authorities, **2** for **private law**, **3** for **criminal law**. **9**, for example, stands for the economy. This way you find rules on one topic together, even if they were made at different times.

The **Federal Constitution** of 18 April 1999 is listed under **SR 101**. Under **SR 210** you find the **Civil Code**. Right after it, under **SR 220**, comes the **Code of Obligations**. If you know these numbers, you can find the most important laws quickly.

Treaties with other states have a **0** placed in front. The **European Convention on Human Rights**, for example, has the number **0.101**. This is how **international law** is told apart from **domestic law**. Within international law, the same order by subject area applies again.

Laws change again and again. That is why the electronic SR is **updated continuously**. So it always shows the **current version**. New acts and changes are first published in the **Official Compilation** and then worked into the SR.

gewusst: The Criminal Code has the number SR 311.0.
The SR exists in German, French and Italian, and important acts also in Romansh and English.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Trade Association, SGV for short, is the umbrella organisation of Switzerland's small and medium-sized enterprises. These include, for example, bakeries, joiners' workshops, hairdressing salons and engineering offices. It was founded in 1879 and has its headquarters in Bern.
wichtigste: The SGV represents small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
SMEs have fewer than 250 employees.
Over 99 per cent of Swiss companies are SMEs.
The SGV was founded in 1879 and has its headquarters in Bern.
It fights for less bureaucracy and lower regulatory costs.
It is strongly committed to dual vocational training.

abschnitte.text: **SME** stands for small and medium-sized enterprises. According to the Federal Statistical Office, these are companies with fewer than **250 employees**. Larger companies are called large enterprises. Over 99 per cent of all companies in Switzerland are SMEs. The SGV is their **umbrella organisation** and represents their concerns in politics.

The Trade Association was founded in **1879**. This makes it a little older than the Swiss Trade Union Federation. Its headquarters are in **Bern**, near the Federal Palace. So it is close to what happens in politics. Every year it holds the “Trade Winter Conference” in **Klosters**. There, representatives of trade and politicians discuss economic policy.

An important concern of the SGV is **reducing regulatory costs**. Rules and forms are often a bigger burden for small firms than for large ones. After all, a small business has no department of its own to deal with them. The SGV therefore campaigns for less regulation and lower administrative costs.

A large share of apprenticeships are offered by SMEs. That is why **dual vocational training** is very important to the SGV. “Dual” means twofold: you learn at the **training company** and at the **vocational school**. The association also publishes a newspaper, the **Schweizerische Gewerbezeitung**.

gewusst: Almost all companies in Switzerland are SMEs: over 99 per cent.
The Trade Association is a year older than the Swiss Trade Union Federation.

teile.einleitung: UNICEF is the children's fund of the United Nations (UN). All over the world it works to make sure that children grow up healthy, can go to school and are protected.
wichtigste: UNICEF belongs to the UN and helps children in many countries.
UNICEF was founded on 11 December 1946, shortly after the Second World War.
Its headquarters are in New York, where the UN also has its headquarters.
UNICEF relies on voluntary contributions from states and on donations.
In 1965 UNICEF received the Nobel Peace Prize.
The light blue logo shows a mother holding up her child in front of a globe.
UNICEF Switzerland and Liechtenstein is based in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: After the **Second World War**, many children in Europe were hungry, ill or had no home any more. That is why on 11 December 1946 the UN founded an aid organisation for children. At first it was mainly about **emergency aid** with food, milk and clothes. Later UNICEF extended its work to the whole world. Today it helps especially in countries where many children live in poverty.

UNICEF makes sure that children get **vaccinations**. Vaccinations protect against dangerous diseases such as measles. The organisation also brings clean water, food and medicine to emergency areas. It supports schools so that more children learn to read and write. UNICEF also campaigns for **children's rights**, which are set out in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.

UNICEF's logo is **light blue**, like the colour of the United Nations. It shows an adult, usually seen as a mother, holding up a child. Behind them you can see a **globe** with olive branches, as in the UN emblem. The picture means: UNICEF protects children all over the world. You can recognise the logo on aid supplies, posters and appeals for donations.

UNICEF does not get fixed money from the UN budget, but relies on **voluntary contributions**. These come from states, companies and many individual people. In many countries there are national committees that collect donations and provide information. The committee **UNICEF Switzerland and Liechtenstein** is based in Zurich. School classes and children help too, for example with collections or sponsored runs.

gewusst: The name UNICEF comes from “United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund”.
UNICEF is one of the few organisations to have received the Nobel Peace Prize, namely in 1965.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Employers' Association represents employers, that is, companies that hire people. It deals with questions about the labour market, education and social insurance. Its counterpart is the trade unions.
wichtigste: The association was founded in 1908 and has its headquarters in Zurich.
It is an umbrella organisation of industry and regional employers' organisations.
It deals with the labour market, education and social policy.
It represents Swiss employers in the International Labour Organization.
It relies on social partnership with the trade unions.
It usually opposes minimum wages set by law.

abschnitte.text: The Employers' Association is an **umbrella organisation**. Its members are mainly **industry associations**, regional employers' organisations and a few individual companies. Together they represent a large share of the people employed in Switzerland. The association has its headquarters in **Zurich**.

The association was founded in **1908** as the “Central Association of Swiss Employers' Organisations”. It was a reaction to the trade unions, which were growing stronger at the time. It kept this old name until 1996. Today it is called the Swiss Employers' Association.

In Switzerland, employers and trade unions often negotiate wages and working conditions themselves. This is called **social partnership**. The results are usually set out in **collective labour agreements**, GAV for short. The state only steps in to add to them. That is why the Employers' Association usually opposes **minimum wages** set by law. For example, it fought against the minimum wage initiative of 2014. The trade unions see it differently and call for minimum wages.

The **AVS** and the pension fund (**BVG**) are largely funded through contributions from wages. Employers and employees pay these together. That is why the Employers' Association has a strong say in pension reforms. **Vocational training** is also important to it, because companies offer many apprenticeships.

The **International Labour Organization** (ILO) has its headquarters in Geneva. It has a three-part structure: governments, employers and workers work together in it. Swiss employers are represented there by the Employers' Association.

gewusst: In the International Labour Organization in Geneva, states, employers and workers sit at one table.
The Employers' Association was founded because the trade unions were becoming stronger and stronger.

teile.einleitung: After every vote, the votes have to be counted. Only then do you know which proposal has won. For the result to be right, you count carefully, honestly and preferably in pairs.
wichtigste: After a vote, you first count the **votes**.
The person who counts the votes is called a **vote counter**.
Counting in pairs is more accurate, because you check each other.
You sort the papers into **piles** for yes and no.
There must never be more votes than voters.
Every vote is equally important.

abschnitte.text: After a vote, there are lots of papers in the **ballot box**. Only when you have counted them all do you know the result. In votes there are **vote counters** for this. They count every vote carefully and honestly. After all, every vote is equally important.

It is best to make two **piles**: one for yes and one for no. Then you count each pile. Often two children count together so that nobody miscounts. They check each other, so mistakes are noticed quickly. In the municipalities too, several people always count together.

If yes has 9 votes and no has 8 votes, then **9 plus 8 equals 17** children have voted. You compare this number with the number of children in the class. If there are 22 children in the class but only 21 papers in the ballot box, one child did not vote. That is allowed. This is how you can check whether everything adds up.
